newsitem.title: GERMANY: Moscow still unhappy on NATO growth-Chernomyrdin.
newsitem.headline: Moscow still unhappy on NATO growth-Chernomyrdin.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Thursday that Moscow still had a negative attitude towards NATO enlargement despite having acceded to the alliance's plan to admit new members from eastern Europe.
"The expansion of the alliance has already had a negative impact on the situation in Europe," Chernomyrdin told the Berliner Zeitung newspaper in an interview.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin opened the way for NATO to take in new members when he signed a Founding Act in Paris at the end of May establishing a constructive relationship between Moscow and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

Leaders of NATO states will decide at a summit in Madrid next week which countries to admit, with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic seen as certainties. U.S. resistance has dampened Romania's and Slovenia's hopes of early membership.

Chernomyrdin, who arrived in Berlin on Thursday for a two-day visit, said any possible future NATO enlargement taking in the former Soviet republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania "would further exacerbate the situation".
Extracts of the newspaper interview were released before publication on Friday.

Chernomyrdin met President Roman Herzog in his Bellevue Palace in Berlin and then laid a wreath at the Soviet memorial in the city's Tiergarten park. On Friday both Chernomyrdin and Chancellor Helmut Kohl are due to address a conference on Russia's future before holding talks.

In the interview, Chernomyrdin praised "the excellent and trusting" relationship between Kohl and Yeltsin, and added that ties with Bonn would play a crucial role in completing Russia's transition to a stable democratic market economy.
Chernomyrdin, however, urged German companies to step up investment in Russia or risk being overtaken by the booming countries of south and southeast Asia.
Chernomyrdin also said he expected Europe to remain a long-term market for Russian natural gas.
In Moscow, the Interfax news agency quoted the government press service as saying Chernomyrdin's visit would cover bilateral trade and economic issues.
One key issue will be the extension of supply contracts for Russian natural gas beyond their current expiry date of 2000, as well as the possible construction of a new east-west gas pipeline.
